Sole Proprietorship 2. Partnership 3. Limited Liability Companies (LLC) 4. S-Corporations Corporate Taxpayers: Profits go to corporation, who pays taxes. Shareholders are also taxed on dividends, resulting in double taxes 1. C-Corporations 4 TYPES OF BUSINESS + DRAWBACKS Sole Proprietorship – One individual owning a business ▪ Advantages: Low regulation, easy to form, and no corporate income taxes ▪ Disadvantages: Limited lifespan, unlimited liability, hard to raise capital, no distinction in assets Partnership– Multiple individuals owning a business ▪ Advantages: Low regulation, easy to form, and no corporate income taxes ▪ Disadvantages: Limited lifespan, unlimited liability, hard to raise capital, no distinction in assets S-Corporation/LLC– Corporations that get taxed like partnerships/proprietorships ▪ Advantages: Lifespan, limited liability protection, and no corporate income taxes ▪ Disadvantages: Restrictions, harder to raise capital compared to C-corp C-Corporation– Corporations, that exist as a separate legal entity ▪ Advantages: Unlimited life, easy transfer, limited liability, ease of raising capital ▪ Disadvantages: Double taxation, higher regulation, cost of set up and filing CHAPTER 1/4 NOTES ON THE FINANCIAL STATEMENTS When you create them, do it in this order:  Income Statement, Balance Sheet, Statement of Stockholders’ Equity, Statement of Cash Flows Places to check your work  (BS): Total Assets = Total Liabilities + Total Equity  Total Stockholders’ Equity (BS) = Total of all columns (SSE)  Cash Account Balances (BS) = Cash Balances (SCF) It sounds obvious, but remember, if they are not equal across statements, you probably added incorrectly somewhere USERS OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS Managers and Employers Investment Analysts and Information Intermediaries Research Reports Creditors and Suppliers • Need to know company’s current financial situation. Contributes to decisions on loaning goods or not Stockholders and Directors • Also invested in company’s financial health. Helps drives stock prices, determine safety of investment CHAPTER 1 P1-9ACCOUNTING STANDARDS AND SEC FILINGS The set of American Accounting Standards are called… What are the benefits of having such standards? Public Companies must publish unaudited quarterly reports with summary versions the four financial statements called… Annually, they must publish audited versions of the entirety of the 4 financial statements with explanatory notes called… GOOD AUDIT OPINION The audit report is not a guarantee that no misstatements exist. Auditors only provide reasonable assurance that the statements are free of material misstatements  Reasonable: not held to an absolute standard if problems are uncovered  Material: item must be of sufficient magnitude (such as a decision to purchase stock or extend credit) SIMPLE RATIO ANALYSIS CATEGORIES Liquidity: Ability for a company to pay its short-term obligations • Current Ratio: Current Assets/Current Liabilities Solvency: Ability for a company to pay its long-term financial obligations • Debt to Assets: Debts/Assets Profitability: Analysis of a company’s profit • Profit Margin: Net Income / Net Sales CHAPTER 2 Accounting cycle steps Permanent vs temporary accounts Accounting terms: Account, element, financial statement line, general ledger, source document ACCOUNTING KEY TERMS Account – a record of the increases and decreases in a specific asset, liability, or equity item Element – One of the three elements of the accounting equation (assets, liabilities or equity) Source Document – records that are generated when a firm engages in a business transaction Chart of Accounts – all the account titles in a business’ accounting system General Ledger – listing of each of a business’ accounts and amounts from all transactions recorded during a period ACCOUNTING CYCLE STEPS STEP 1: Analyze transactions • Make sure that your transaction will balance on the balance sheet. STEP 2: Record transactions in the accounting records 1. A transaction will impact the cash flow statement iff it impacts cash on the balance sheet 2. Any transaction that increases/decreases net income impacts retained earnings 3. Dividends impact retained earnings, but not the income statement STEP 3: Adjust transactions. This will never impact cash. STEP 4: Prepare Financial Statements (income Statement -> Balance Sheet -> Statement of Stockholders’ Equity -> Statement of Cash Flows) STEP 5: Close the temporary accounts in anticipation of the start of a new accounting cycle PERMANENT VS TEMPORARY ACCOUNTS Temporary Accounts  Balances are zero at the start of each accounting period  Income statement (revenues and expenses) and the dividend account Permanent Account  Accounts carry over from period to period  Balance sheet CHAPTER 2 SE2-2CHAPTER 2 E2-6CHAPTER 2 P2-5 CHAPTER 3 Accrual accounting Revenue recognition principle Expense recognition principle Quality of earnings What is a trial balance Debits & Credits – (multiple choice only) Record transactions – financial statement effects (workout problem)  Must know balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow impact Adjusting entries • Must know balance sheet, income statement, and cash flow impact Closing entries – debit/credits (multiple choice only) ACCRUAL ACCOUNTING An accounting method where revenues/expenses are recorded when a transaction occurs Requires adjustments to be made to reconcile current status of the balance sheet REVENUE RECOGNITION PRINCIPLE Recognize revenues for goods and services provided to customers at an amount expected to be received  This may be before the company actually receives the cash, i.e., when they bill a customer for a service or good, they recognize the income at that time  Must be at the time that, or after, the company satisfies the obligation by delivering the good(s) or service(s) Revenue Related Accounts: Cash, Unearned Revenue, Accounts Recievable EXPENSE RECOGNITION PRINCIPLE Expenses shall be recognized when they are incurred  This may be before the expense is actually paid for (cash exchanges hands) Expense Related Accounts: Prepaid Expense, Supplies, PPE, Accounts Payable (or any ___ Payable), Cash QUALITY OF EARNINGS How well a company’s earnings report represents its underlying financial performance. Especially in regard to adjustments. Good QOE: Adjustments accurately reflect the companies financial health Conservative QOE: Adjustments are pessimistic, leading to lower net income + assets ▪ Generally preferred by investors, since these will remain consistent YoY Ways to measure QOE 1. Financial Statement Transaction Model 2. T-Accounts 3. Journal Entries ADJUSTING ENTRIES Prepaid Expenses  Cash is paid before expenses are recognized  Insurance, rent Unearned Revenues  Cash is received before the revenues area recognized  Girl Scout sold cookies and collected cash before she delivers them Accrued Expenses  Cash is paid after the expense is recognized  Paying a Credit Card bill Accrued Revenues  Cash is received after the revenue is recognized  You worked ten hours last week, but you will not be paid until next week PREPAID EXPENSESUNEARNED REVENUESACCRUED EXPENSESACCRUED REVENUESCHAPTER 3 Q3-5CHAPTER 3 SE3-5CHAPTER 3 P3-6DEBITS AND CREDITS Dividends, Expenses, Assets  Debit = Increase  Credit = Decrease Liabilities, Equity, Revenue  Debit = Decrease  Credit = Increase Normal balance is side you increase on TRIAL BALANCE A listing of all general ledger accounts and their respective credits and debit balances Prepared at the end of an accounting period after all transactions are recorded amount of debits = amount of credits CLOSING ENTRIES **Close INCOME STATEMENT accounts (Sales/Revenue, COGS, expenses, dividends) Move Net Sales to Retained Earnings Move Money from Retained Earnings to cover losses and expenses Move Money from retained earnings to cover dividends APPENDIX C EC-1APPENDIX C EC-3 CHAPTER 5 Fraud Fraud triangle Internal controls COSO framework Audit opinion related to internal controls PCAOB What is considered cash Good cash controls Bank reconciliations FRAUD + FRAUD TRIANGLE Fraud – Intentionally misreporting a company’s financial statements for personal or corporate gain INTERNAL CONTROLS Internal Controls – Management’s responsibility to prevent errors + deter fraud by:  Safeguarding assets, providing accurate information, promoting efficiency, enforcing policies, and complying with regulations Types of Internal Controls: 1. Preventative Controls: Stopping problems before they happen (ex. Payment Authorization) 2. Detective Controls: Finds problems after they happen (ex. Bank Adjustments Audit Opinion’s for Internal Controls – Since SOX Act, companies must report on design/effectiveness of their internal control. Accounting firms also give audit opinions on the design/effectiveness of internal controls Public Company Accounting Oversight Board – Issues auditing standards, oversees quality controls on public accounting firms COSO FRAMEWORK 1. Control Environment – setting the tone of the organization to be ethical 2. Risk Assessment – identifying and analyzing risks that face the organization 3. Control Activities – the specific policies designed to reduce risk (internal controls) 4. Information and Communication – making sure management and employees are on same page 5. Monitoring Activities – assessing internal system, evaluating its effectiveness CASH + GOOD CASH CONTROLS Cash - Checks, Currency, Money account orders, Checking account balance, Saving account balance Cash Equivalent – Highly Liquid assets, Short term investments (<90 days), Risk free securities Good Cash Controls: Clear policies, separation of duties, bank reconciliation  Receipts: Record at bank when received, Deposit at bank daily, Count cash frequently, Give customers receipts  Disbursements: Pay with checks (prenumbered), Segregate duties, Require signatures and documentation on larger amounts BANK RECONCILIATION Reconciling the book balances with the bank balances Terms: 1. Bank statement debit memos -Reduce customers account balance -Bank Fee 2. Bank statement credit memos Increase customers account balance - Interest earned 3. Outstanding checks - Checks written by company, not yet received by bank 4. Deposits in Transit -Deposits not yet recorded by bank CHAPTER 5 E5-5 CHAPTER 5 E5-3 CHAPTER 11 Vertical analysis Horizontal analysis Financial ratios Liquidity Solvency Profitability Interest in Ratios Cash conversion cycle VERTICAL VERSUS HORIZONTAL ANALYSIS Vertical Analysis  Expresses financial statements in ratio form  Income in terms of percent of net sales, balance sheet in terms of percent of total assets  AKA Common Size Financial Statements  Useful to comparing companies of different sizes Horizontal Analysis  Expresses changes in financial statements across time  Allows for the identification of trends within a company  Used to compare a company to itself during different accounting cycles LIQUIDITY Liquidity refers to cash availability; How much a company has and how quickly it can be accessed/raised on short notice  Current Ratio  Liquidity based on Current Assets and Current Liabilities  Quick Ratio  Liquidity based on Cash, Marketable Securities, Accounts Receivable; Only the most liquid current assets SOLVENCY Solvency refers to a company’s ability to meet its debt obligations (interest payments and loan repayments)  Liabilities-To-Equity  Tells how reliant a company is on its creditor financing (loans) compared to equity (stock investors)  Interest Coverage Ratio  Core profits to liabilities, meet debt obligation based on income PROFITABILITY VERSUS EFFICIENCY Profitability:  Assessed by looking at Profit Margin  How profitable is each dollar that is being spent?  Ex: Gross profit margin/operating expense margin/profit margin Efficiency/Productivity:  Assessed by looking at Asset Turnover  How productive are a company’s assets in generating sales?  Ex: Cash conversion cycle/PPE turnover CASH CONVERSION CYCLE Number of Days the company has its cash tied up in receivable and inventories less the number of days of trade credit provided by company suppliers Average Days in Sales Outstanding +Average Days in Inventory Outstanding -Average Days Payable Outstanding =Average Cash Conversion Cycle INTEREST IN RATIOS + CCC Ratios are useful to both internal and external users, as a quantifying measure of a company’s performance in a specific category  Ex. Short term lenders would be interested in a company's liquidity ratios, long term lenders would be interested in a company’s solvency ratios Cash Conversion Cycle measures how fast companies turn investments in inventory into cash  Negative CCC means you are selling goods before paying supplier  Long CCC (>60 days) means you are converting inventory to cash slowly  Smaller CCC indicates business efficiency, converting inventory to cash fast CHAPTER 4 E4-5CHAPTER 11 E11-5CCC PROBLEM FROM LAST YEAR!
